title: 15 ECTS of Finnish, Fast: The Smartest Routes for Expats in Finland
description: How to Get 15 Credits in Finnish as Quickly as Possible in Finland From open studies to flexible course options, here’s how to reach the credit target without making it harder than it…
html:
How to Get 15 Credits in Finnish as Quickly as Possible in Finland

From open studies to flexible course options, here’s how to reach the credit target without making it harder than it needs to be.

If you need to complete 15 ECTS credits in Finnish language studies as soon as possible, you are not alone. Many international students and professionals in Finland need Finnish credits for degree requirements, residence permit conditions, integration plans, or employment eligibility. The good news is that there are several legitimate and relatively fast ways to complete 15 credits, but the best option depends on your current status (degree student, exchange student, job seeker, or working professional) and your timeline.

This guide walks you through the fastest and most reliable options available in Finland, how they work, and what to consider before enrolling.

First: What Does 15 ECTS Credits Mean in Practice?

In Finland, 1 ECTS credit represents approximately 27 hours of work. Therefore:

15 ECTS ≈ 400 hours of total work (including contact teaching, assignments, and self-study).

In practical terms, 15 credits usually equals:
– Three separate 5-credit courses, or
– One intensive 15-credit module, or
– A combination of courses completed over one or two teaching periods.

The fastest realistic completion time is usually one academic semester (about 3–4 months), although intensive summer or period-based courses may allow you to complete them more quickly.

Option 1: Finnish Courses Through a University (Fastest for Degree Students)

If you are already enrolled in a Finnish university or university of applied sciences (UAS), this is typically the fastest and most straightforward route.

Most Finnish higher education institutions offer:

– Finnish for beginners (A1 level)
– Intermediate Finnish (A2–B1)
– Academic Finnish
– Finnish for specific fields (e.g., healthcare, business, engineering)

These courses are usually worth 3–5 ECTS each. Completing three 5-credit courses in one semester is very realistic, especially if you prioritize your schedule.

Advantages:
– Recognized academic credits
– Usually free for degree students
– Structured progression
– Official transcript entry

If you need credits urgently, contact:
– The language center (kielikeskus)
– Your study advisor
– The international office

Ask specifically:
“Can I complete 15 ECTS in Finnish within one or two periods?”

Some institutions allow intensive courses during one teaching period (around 7–8 weeks), making it possible to earn 10–15 credits within a single semester if you take multiple parallel courses.

Option 2: Open University (Avoin Yliopisto) – Flexible and Fast

If you are not currently a degree student, Open University programs are one of the best options.

Open Universities (offered by nearly all Finnish universities) allow anyone to enroll in courses for a fee, regardless of degree status. Finnish language courses are commonly available.

Typical characteristics:
– 3–5 ECTS per course
– Online and in-person options
– Fees typically range from 15–25 euros per credit

Many Open Universities offer intensive courses during:
– Autumn (Period I & II)
– Spring (Period III & IV)
– Summer sessions

Summer courses are often the fastest route. It is sometimes possible to complete 10–15 ECTS during a single summer term (May–August), especially if you combine two intensive courses.

Well-known providers include:
– University of Helsinki Open University
– University of Turku Open University
– Tampere University Open University
– University of Oulu Open University

Make sure the course description explicitly states the number of ECTS credits and that you will receive an official transcript.

Option 3: Universities of Applied Sciences (UAS / AMK)

Universities of Applied Sciences also offer Finnish language courses, both for their students and sometimes through their open studies platforms.

These courses are often:
– Practical and work-oriented
– Focused on professional Finnish
– Structured in 5 ECTS modules

If you are aiming to work in Finland in fields like healthcare, engineering, business, or IT, UAS courses can be particularly useful.

Some UAS institutions also offer:
– Online intensive Finnish
– Hybrid models (online + classroom)
– Fast-track beginner programs

Check whether the credits are recognized by your institution if you are transferring them elsewhere.

Option 4: Integration Training (Kotoutumiskoulutus)

If you are registered as unemployed and have an integration plan through TE Services, you may be offered integration training.

However, there is an important distinction:

Integration courses usually do not automatically provide ECTS credits unless they are specifically connected to a higher education institution.

Some programs are delivered in cooperation with universities or UAS institutions and may provide credits, but many do not. Always verify:

“Will I receive official ECTS credits and a transcript?”

If you specifically need 15 ECTS credits, standard integration training may not meet that requirement.

Option 5: Fully Online Academic Courses

Some universities offer online Finnish language courses for credit. These are particularly useful if:

– You live outside major cities
– You work full time
– You need flexibility

Online courses can sometimes be completed more quickly because they are asynchronous. However, they still require substantial work.

Be cautious with private language schools. Many offer excellent teaching, but unless they are affiliated with an accredited higher education institution, they do not issue ECTS credits.

If credits are essential, confirm:
– Is this course officially worth X ECTS?
– Will I receive a transcript from a Finnish higher education institution?

How Fast Is “ASAP” Realistically?

If your goal is pure speed, here is what is realistic:

Best-case scenario:
You enroll in three 5 ECTS intensive courses during one semester (about 3–4 months).

Very fast scenario:
You complete 10 ECTS during one intensive period and 5 ECTS during summer.

Extremely fast (rare but possible):
An intensive summer block offering 15 ECTS over 2–3 months.

Completing 15 legitimate ECTS credits in just a few weeks is not realistic due to the workload requirement.

How to Choose the Right Option

Ask yourself:

1. Do I need the credits for a degree requirement?
2. Do I need them for immigration or residence permit reasons?
3. Am I currently enrolled at a Finnish institution?
4. Do I need beginner-level Finnish, or can I take higher-level courses?
5. Can I study full time for one semester?

If you are already a degree student, your university’s language center is almost always the fastest route.

If you are not a student, Open University is usually the most flexible and reliable option.

Important: Verify Credit Transferability

Before enrolling, confirm:

– Will these credits count toward my specific degree?
– Does my institution accept Open University credits?
– Is there a level requirement (e.g., must reach A2 or B1)?

Getting 15 credits quickly is helpful only if they are officially recognized where you need them.

Cost Expectations

If you are a degree student:
Usually free.

If you use Open University:
Expect approximately 225–375 euros total for 15 credits.

Private language schools:
Prices may be higher, and credits are usually not official ECTS unless partnered with a university.

Recommended Strategy for Fastest Completion

If speed is your top priority, here is a practical strategy:

1. Search Open University websites for upcoming intensive Finnish courses.
2. Register early because popular courses fill quickly.
3. Combine two courses in one period and one in the next.
4. Confirm transcript issuance.
5. Dedicate sufficient weekly study hours (15–25 hours per week).

This approach typically allows completion within one semester.

Final Thoughts

It is absolutely possible to complete 15 ECTS credits in Finnish within one semester in Finland, and sometimes even faster during intensive periods. The key is choosing an accredited provider, verifying credit recognition in advance, and committing the necessary time.

title: Can a Grandparent Take Your Child to a Finnish Embassy Appointment? What You Need (and What People Forget)
description: If both parents are in Finland and your child is doing their appointment abroad with a relative, here’s what usually matters: consent, guardianship proof, legalised documents, and the…
html:
If both parents are in Finland and your child is doing their appointment abroad with a relative, here’s what usually matters: consent, guardianship proof, legalised documents, and the country-by-country extras that can catch you out.

If you’re reading this two weeks before the appointment, slightly panicking, you’re not alone. The good news: in most straightforward cases, a grandparent can accompany a child to the appointment. The key is making sure the embassy/VFS can clearly see:

  1. Who the child is (identity check)

  2. Who the legal guardians are (custody/guardianship)

  3. That the guardians consent to the application and the visit (signed consent)

For Finnish residence permits, Migri decides the application, but the child still has to show up in person at the mission/VFS for identity and biometrics.

First: what kind of appointment is it?

This matters, because the rules and “strictness” vary by application type.

1) Residence permit (family ties)

This is the most common for children living abroad while parents are in Finland. The application is submitted by the parent/guardian (usually in Enter Finland), and the child attends the appointment to prove identity and provide biometrics.

2) D visa (linked to a residence permit)

Still tied to a residence permit process. Requirements are mission-specific, but the same principle applies: identity, documents, consent.

3) Schengen visa (short stay)

These often have stricter “guardian presence/consent” requirements in local checklists (and they can be picky about consent wording and verification).

If your situation is “child abroad, parents in Finland, child moving to Finland”, you’re almost always in residence permit based on family ties territory.

Do you need a power of attorney for the grandparent?

Usually: no, not just to accompany

If you (the parents/legal guardians) have already submitted the application, the appointment is mainly about the child’s identity, originals, and biometrics. The person walking the child into the building typically isn’t making the legal decisions.

When a power of attorney is relevant

A power of attorney comes into play if someone else is actually submitting the application on your behalf (rather than just accompanying the child). Enter Finland explicitly says a person authorised by power of attorney can submit a child’s application.

So: accompanying ≠ submitting.

What you should do instead: bring a clear consent letter

Even when a power of attorney isn’t required, a signed consent letter from both parents is one of those “tiny effort, huge hassle avoided” documents.

Migri’s guidance is clear that both parents must sign the child’s residence permit application or provide written consent (and for online applications, consent can be attached as a signed document).

Consent letter should include:

  • Full names + passport details of both parents

  • Child’s full name + date of birth + passport number

  • Grandparent’s full name + ID/passport number

  • Statement that the grandparent is authorised to accompany the child to the Finnish embassy/VFS for the appointment (date + location)

  • Both parents’ signatures + date + contact details

Tip: Some missions/VFS centres like this notarised. It is not always required, but if you can notarise it easily, it can reduce arguments at the counter.

The “don’t-get-turned-away” document checklist

For a child’s residence permit application, Enter Finland lists core attachments like:

  • Child’s passport

  • Birth certificate (with parents)

  • Guardianship/custody documentation (if applicable)

  • Translations (if not Finnish/Swedish/English)

  • Legalisation for official certificates (if not Nordic/EU)

Practical pack for the appointment (works in most countries)

Bring originals + copies of:

  • Child’s passport

  • Child’s birth certificate (showing parents)

  • Custody/guardianship documents (if relevant)

  • Appointment confirmation + application reference/receipt

  • Consent letter signed by both parents (plus copies of parents’ passports/residence permits in Finland)

  • Any Migri/Enter Finland request letters (if you’ve received them)

Legalisation and translation: the bit that causes the most delays

If your documents are issued outside the Nordic/EU area, legalisation is commonly required, and translations usually need to be done properly. Enter Finland notes:

  • Official certificates may need legalisation if not Nordic/EU

  • If documents aren’t in Finnish/Swedish/English, they need an authorised translation

Finland’s DVV also explains the general rule: documents typically need Apostille/legalisation unless EU/Nordic, and translations may need to be legalised or done by an authorised translator.

This is where different countries really diverge, so if you do one thing today: check the mission/VFS page for that country.

“But we’re in Finland and the child is abroad” – does that change anything?

Not really, except it makes the consent paperwork even more useful.

Also remember: the child must be present when submitting/proving identity for a first residence permit.

What about travel rules (not the embassy appointment)?

Separate issue, but worth thinking ahead: many border authorities and airlines may ask for parental travel consent when a child travels with someone who isn’t a parent/legal guardian.

Finland’s Ministry for Foreign Affairs advises that when a minor travels without a parent/guardian, it’s sensible to carry written parental consent, because other countries’ authorities may request it.

This is not Kenya-specific. It’s a “any country might ask, airlines might ask” situation.

The safe, simple plan (works for most countries)

  1. Write a consent letter (both parents sign)

  2. Add copies of both parents’ IDs and proof you live in Finland

  3. Ensure birth certificate/custody docs are translated + legalised if required

  4. Check the local Finnish mission/VFS instructions for that country

  5. Send the grandparent with originals + copies in a tidy folder

title: Is Ammattikoulu Actually Free for Non-EU Residents? Tuition Fees, Permits, and What People Get Wrong
description: Who pays (and who doesn’t), how your permit type changes the answer, and what to check before you apply so you don’t get surprised later. If you are currently in Finland, studying…
html:
Who pays (and who doesn’t), how your permit type changes the answer, and what to check before you apply so you don’t get surprised later.

If you are currently in Finland, studying Finnish and planning to start ammattikoulu (vocational upper secondary education), it is completely understandable to feel unsure about tuition rules, especially after hearing different things about non‑EU students and fees.

The good news is that vocational education in Finland operates under different rules than universities and universities of applied sciences. Below is a clear, fact‑checked explanation of how it works and what applies in your situation.

1. Is Ammattikoulu Free for Non‑EU Residents?

In most cases, yes. Vocational upper secondary education (ammatillinen koulutus) in Finland is tuition‑free regardless of nationality.

Unlike universities and universities of applied sciences, which charge tuition fees to non‑EU/EEA students studying in English, vocational education does not generally charge tuition fees based on citizenship.

If you are legally residing in Finland and admitted to a publicly funded vocational institution, the education itself is free of tuition fees.

This applies whether you are:
– An EU citizen
– A non‑EU citizen
– A refugee
– A family member of a worker
– On a student residence permit

Nationality alone does not determine tuition fees in vocational education.

What Is Actually Free?

Vocational education funded by the Finnish government covers:
– Teaching
– Guidance and counselling
– Personal study planning
– Many learning materials

Students may still need to pay for some items themselves, such as:
– Tools, work clothing or safety shoes (depending on the field)
– Personal equipment
– Travel costs
– Optional materials

But there is no standard tuition fee charged simply because you are non‑EU.

2. Does It Depend on the Type of Residence Permit?

This is where confusion often arises.

In higher education (universities and UAS), tuition fees apply to non‑EU students who come to Finland specifically on a student residence permit.

However, vocational education works differently.

For vocational upper secondary education:

– There is no automatic tuition fee for non‑EU citizens.
– Your residence status does not automatically trigger tuition.
– What matters more is whether you are legally residing in Finland and admitted to a publicly funded institution.

That said, there are a few practical considerations:

If You Are Already Living in Finland

If you already:
– Have a valid residence permit
– Are registered in the Population Information System
– Have a municipality of residence (kotikunta)

Then vocational education is generally tuition‑free.

If You Apply From Outside Finland

If someone applies from abroad and does not yet have residence status in Finland, the situation can vary. In some cases:
– The school may require proof of residence rights.
– Admission may depend on whether you can legally reside in Finland.
– Residence permit approval is required before studies can begin.

But again, this is about immigration status, not tuition fees charged because of nationality.

3. What If You Have a Dependent Residence Permit?

If you hold a residence permit as a family member (for example, as the dependent of someone with a work‑based residence permit), vocational education is generally free.

In fact, this is one of the most common situations.

If you:
– Live in Finland legally
– Have a valid residence permit as a family member
– Are registered with a municipality of residence

You are typically treated the same way as other residents when it comes to vocational upper secondary education.

There is no separate tuition category for dependents of workers.

4. The Key Factor: Municipality of Residence (Kotikunta)

In Finland, many education rights are tied not just to residence permits, but to having a municipality of residence (kotikunta).

If you are registered as living in a Finnish municipality, you are part of the publicly funded education system. This is what usually ensures your access to tuition‑free vocational education.

If someone does not have a municipality of residence, the situation may be more complicated and should be clarified directly with the institution.

5. Are There Any Exceptions?

There are a few situations where fees might apply:

1. Private institutions
Some private training providers may charge fees. Always check whether the institution is publicly funded.

2. Special or international programmes
Rarely, special training programmes designed for international recruitment may involve different funding arrangements.

3. Adult education courses outside the qualification system
Some short courses or additional training programs may charge participation fees.

However, standard vocational upper secondary qualifications (ammatillinen perustutkinto) offered by public institutions are tuition‑free.

6. Comparison: Vocational Education vs. University Tuition

To avoid confusion, here is a simple distinction:

Universities and Universities of Applied Sciences:
– Non‑EU students studying in English usually pay tuition fees.
– Fees are typically €6,000–€15,000 per year.

Vocational Upper Secondary Education (Ammattikoulu):
– No general tuition fees based on nationality.
– Publicly funded.
– Free for residents regardless of EU/non‑EU status.

This difference is often the source of misunderstandings.

7. What You Should Do Next

To be completely certain about your specific situation:

1. Contact the admissions office of the ammattikoulu you plan to attend.
2. Confirm that the programme is publicly funded vocational education.
3. Ask whether there are any equipment or material costs.
4. Ensure your residence permit and municipality registration are valid before studies begin.

If you are already in Finland on a legal residence permit and planning to continue your education, it is very likely that your vocational studies will be tuition‑free.

Final Summary

• Ammattikoulu (vocational upper secondary education) in Finland is generally tuition‑free.
• Nationality alone does not determine whether you pay tuition.
• Non‑EU citizens do not automatically pay fees for vocational education.
• Having a dependent residence permit does not prevent you from accessing free vocational education.
• The most important factor is legal residence and typically having a municipality of residence in Finland.

If you are already living in Finland and planning to continue into vocational education, there is a strong chance you will not need to pay tuition fees.

title: Kela Maternity Benefits and the Baby Box: How Long Does the Decision Actually Take (and What to Do After 2 Weeks Turns Into 4)
description: What Kela’s processing times really mean, the common reasons it drags on, and the quickest ways to check status or nudge it along without making it worse. If you have applied for…
html:
What Kela’s processing times really mean, the common reasons it drags on, and the quickest ways to check status or nudge it along without making it worse.

If you have applied for maternity benefits and the famous Kela baby box (äitiyspakkaus), it can be stressful to wait longer than expected for a decision. Many parents notice that Kela’s website may state an estimated processing time of around two weeks, yet in practice the decision can sometimes take longer. If you have been waiting four weeks or more, you are not alone.

Below is a clear explanation of how the system works, typical processing times, and what you can do if your application seems delayed.

Understanding the Two Separate Processes

It is important to understand that there are two related but distinct matters:

1. The decision on maternity allowance (äitiysraha).
2. The decision and delivery of the maternity grant (either the baby box or the cash alternative of €170).

Although these are linked, they may not always be processed at exactly the same speed.

Typical Processing Times

Kela publishes estimated processing times on its website. Under normal circumstances:

• Maternity allowance decisions often take approximately 2–4 weeks.
• The maternity grant (baby box or cash) decision may take a similar amount of time.
• After approval, delivery of the baby box itself can take an additional 1–2 weeks, depending on stock and postal service.

However, these are averages, not guarantees.

In practice, four weeks is still within a normal timeframe, especially during busy periods.

Why Processing May Take Longer

There are several common reasons for delays:

1. High Application Volumes

Processing times often increase during peak periods, especially in spring and autumn when many applications are submitted.

2. Incomplete Applications

If any required information is missing, Kela may pause processing and request additional documents. This can significantly extend the timeline.

Common missing items include:
• Confirmation of pregnancy from a maternity clinic (usually after week 154 of pregnancy)
• Employment or income details
• Clarifications about residence status

3. Residence Status Checks

For expats or recently arrived families, Kela may need to confirm eligibility under the Finnish social security system. This assessment can take additional time, particularly if you have recently moved to Finland or your right of residence is still being processed.

4. Manual Review

Some cases are processed automatically, while others require manual handling by a case officer. Manual reviews naturally take longer.

When Should You Be Concerned?

If:

• It has been more than 6 weeks with no decision
• You have received a request for additional information but already responded
• Your due date is approaching and you have no confirmation

Then it is reasonable to contact Kela directly.

However, at the four-week mark, the situation is still quite common and not usually a cause for alarm.

How to Check Your Application Status

The fastest way to check your situation is through:

• Kela’s online service (OmaKela)
• The Kela mobile app

Log in with your Finnish online banking credentials or mobile ID. You can see:

• Whether your application is being processed
• If additional documents are requested
• An estimated processing date in some cases

If everything shows as received and “in process,” it generally means you simply need to wait.

What If You Need the Decision Urgently?

If there is a genuine urgency (for example, an imminent due date or financial hardship), you can:

• Call Kela’s customer service
• Send a message via OmaKela
• Visit a Kela service point (appointments may be required)

Be prepared to provide your personal identity code and application reference details.

Kela does not usually expedite cases without a clear reason, but they can confirm whether everything is in order.

Important Timing Rules to Remember

To qualify for the maternity grant (baby box or cash), you must:

• Attend a prenatal health check-up before the end of the fourth month of pregnancy.
• Be covered by Finnish social security.

You can apply for the maternity grant once the pregnancy has lasted at least 154 days (about 22 weeks).

Applying promptly after reaching eligibility can help avoid last-minute stress.

For Expats: Additional Considerations

If you are new to Finland, processing may take longer because Kela must determine whether you are permanently residing in Finland under social security legislation.

Factors that influence this include:

• Type of residence permit (if applicable)
• Length and intention of stay
• Employment contract
• EU vs non-EU citizenship

If your Kela coverage decision is still pending, maternity benefit decisions may be delayed until your status is confirmed.

What Happens After Approval?

Once approved:

• If you chose the baby box, you will receive tracking details when it is shipped.
• If you chose the cash alternative, the €170 payment will be transferred directly to your bank account.
• Maternity allowance payments will follow the schedule indicated in your decision letter.

Reassurance: Waiting Four Weeks Is Common

Although official estimates may mention two weeks, four weeks is not unusual, especially during busy periods or if your case requires manual review.

In most cases, no action is needed unless:
• You receive a request for additional documents.
• The wait exceeds six weeks.
• There are urgent circumstances.

Final Advice

If you are currently waiting at the four-week mark, the most likely explanation is normal processing time rather than a problem.

Check OmaKela to confirm that:
• Your application was received.
• No additional documents are requested.

If everything appears in order, patience is usually the best course of action.

Finland’s maternity benefit system is reliable, but it is not always as fast as the minimum estimate shown online. Most families do receive their decision and baby box in good time before the birth.

title: Left Your Bag on the Train in Finland? Here’s How Likely You Are to Get It Back
description: What usually happens next, how long it takes to show up in the system, and the steps that actually improve your chances. Forgetting your bag on a train can trigger immediate panic.…
html:
What usually happens next, how long it takes to show up in the system, and the steps that actually improve your chances.

Forgetting your bag on a train can trigger immediate panic. Whether it contains your laptop, passport, house keys, or simply everyday essentials, the first questions are always the same: Is it gone for good? And what are the chances I’ll actually get it back?

If you left your bag on a train in Finland and have already submitted an online report, the good news is that your chances of recovery are generally quite good, especially compared to many other countries. However, the outcome depends on several practical factors: the train operator, the type of train, how quickly you reported it, and what was inside the bag.

Let’s take a detailed look at how the system works and what realistically affects your chances.

How Lost Property Works on Finnish Trains

In Finland, most long-distance and commuter rail services are operated by VR (Valtion Rautatiet). Local commuter services in the Helsinki region operate under HSL, though the trains themselves are typically run by VR on HSL’s behalf.

When an item is left on a train, it usually follows this path:

1. Cleaning staff find the item at the end of the route.
2. The item is registered and transferred to a central lost property service.
3. It is stored for a legally defined holding period.
4. If unclaimed, it may eventually be auctioned, recycled, or disposed of.

Finland has a well-organised lost property system. Many public transport operators work with professional lost-and-found service providers that catalogue items carefully. This significantly improves the odds of recovery.

How Likely Is Recovery?

While there are no publicly released exact percentages for recovery rates, several practical realities increase your chances in Finland:

Strong social trust culture
Finland consistently ranks among the highest-trust societies globally. Lost wallets and phones are frequently returned intact. Opportunistic theft certainly exists, but it is not the norm.

Low incidence of petty crime on trains
Compared to major metropolitan rail systems elsewhere in Europe, Finnish trains experience relatively low levels of pickpocketing and opportunistic theft.

Structured lost property handling
Items left behind are usually found by cleaning crews rather than other passengers, especially on longer routes. Staff are trained to hand items into the official system.

If your bag was left on a long-distance VR train and you reported it quickly, your chances are generally good, particularly if the bag was not immediately accessible to other passengers (for example, stored on overhead racks rather than next to the aisle).

What Reduces the Chances?

There are, however, factors that can lower the likelihood of recovery:

Valuables visible in the bag
If a laptop, tablet, or high-end electronics were clearly visible, the risk of someone taking the bag before staff found it increases.

Busy commuter routes
Urban commuter trains during rush hour have higher passenger turnover. A bag may be noticed and picked up more quickly by someone else.

Delay in reporting
If you wait several days before reporting, it becomes harder to trace which train and carriage the item was on. Quick reporting significantly improves tracking.

Unclear description
Vague descriptions such as “black bag” make identification difficult. Detailed information increases matching accuracy.

What Happens After You Report Online?

When you submit an online report, your information enters the lost property database. The process typically works like this:

First 1–3 days
The train completes its route. Cleaning crews inspect the carriage. If your bag is found, it is tagged and sent to processing.

Within about a week
The item is registered in the lost property system. If your report matches the description, you may be contacted.

Up to 3 months storage
Items are typically stored for approximately three months, though exact timeframes vary.

It’s important to understand that there is often a delay between the loss and the item appearing in the system. Many people assume it’s gone because they receive no immediate response, but processing can take several days.

Identification and Retrieval

To reclaim your bag, you must prove ownership. This typically involves:

Describing unique contents
Providing ID
Paying a handling or service fee

Yes, even if your bag is returned, you will usually pay a retrieval fee. This covers handling, storage, and administrative costs.

If you cannot collect it in person, delivery may be arranged for an additional fee.

Special Case: Passports and Official Documents

Passports and national ID cards are often handled with extra care. If found, they may be transferred to police authorities rather than stored in general lost property. If you lost your passport, it is wise to contact both the train operator and the police.

Electronics: Higher Risk, But Still Recoverable

Laptops, tablets, and smartphones are more attractive items. However, in Finland, many such items are still handed in. Recovery likelihood increases significantly if:

The device is password protected
There is identifying information inside the bag
You reported the loss quickly

Adding contact information inside your bag dramatically increases the chance of direct return.

Realistic Expectations

If your bag was:

Left on a long-distance train
Reported within 24 hours
Not obviously displaying valuables
Clearly described in your report

Then your odds are reasonably strong.

If your bag was:

Left on a crowded commuter train
Unattended for a long period
Containing visible high-value items
Reported several days later

Then the chances decrease, though recovery is still possible.

What You Should Do Now

If you have already filed the online report:

1. Keep your reference number.
2. Monitor your email (including spam folder).
3. Wait at least several business days before assuming it is lost.
4. Follow up if you receive no response within a week.

If your bag contained bank cards or sensitive documents, immediately cancel cards and monitor accounts. In Finland, precautionary action is advisable even though fraud rates are relatively low.

How Finland Compares Internationally

Compared to many countries, Finland offers above-average recovery prospects. The combination of public trust, efficient public services, and structured lost property systems works in your favour.

This does not guarantee a return. No country can promise that. Still, Finland is one of the better places in Europe to have forgotten something on public transport.

Final Assessment

So how likely are you to get your bag back?

In Finland, the answer is: more likely than you might think.

While there are no guarantees, many lost items, including bags with valuables, are successfully returned every year. If you acted quickly and provided detailed information, there is a realistic and reasonable chance your bag will make its way back to you.

The most difficult part is often the waiting. Processing takes time, and silence does not mean failure.

In Finland, lost does not automatically mean gone.

title: Permanent Residence in Finland: Do You Need 15 Credits of Finnish, and What Counts as Proof of Language Skills?
description: What Migri counts as “language proof” now, what your AMK degree covers (and what it doesn’t), and the quickest ways to tick the box without doing extra studies for no reason. Many…
html:
What Migri counts as “language proof” now, what your AMK degree covers (and what it doesn’t), and the quickest ways to tick the box without doing extra studies for no reason.

Many international students in Finland are currently confused about whether the rules for permanent residence (PR) have changed, especially regarding Finnish language requirements. This is particularly relevant for students completing degrees in Finnish and for those with vocational qualifications.

Below is a clear and up‑to‑date explanation of how the rules work, what has changed, and what actually counts as proof of language skills.

1. Is There a Language Requirement for Permanent Residence?

As of the current legislation in force, a permanent residence permit (P permit) in Finland does not automatically require you to demonstrate Finnish or Swedish language skills.

Traditionally, the key requirements for a permanent residence permit have been:

• Four years of continuous residence in Finland with an A (continuous) permit
• No significant breaks in residence
• No serious criminal record
• The grounds for your previous permit still being valid

Unlike Finnish citizenship, permanent residence has not required passing a language test.

However, the Finnish government has proposed changes to tighten immigration rules. These proposals include:

• Extending the required period of residence (for example, from four to six years)
• Introducing a language requirement (likely at level A2 or B1)

Some of these changes are expected to enter into force between 2025 and 2026, but implementation depends on final legislative approval and transition periods.

Because the situation is evolving, you should always check the Finnish Immigration Service (Migri) website for the exact rules in force at the time you apply.

2. If My Degree Is Fully in Finnish at a University of Applied Sciences, Do I Need Separate 15 Credits of Finnish?

If your entire degree at a Finnish university of applied sciences (UAS) is completed in Finnish, you generally do not need separate 15 ECTS credits of Finnish language studies to prove language proficiency.

There is no general rule in the permanent residence system requiring a separate 15-credit Finnish language module.

Where confusion often arises is in relation to citizenship applications. For Finnish citizenship, language proficiency can be proven in several ways, including:

• Completing a comprehensive school education in Finnish or Swedish
• Completing upper secondary education in Finnish or Swedish
• Completing a vocational qualification in Finnish or Swedish
• Completing a bachelor’s or master’s degree in Finnish or Swedish
• Passing the National Certificate of Language Proficiency (YKI) at level 3 (B1)

If your entire higher education degree is conducted and assessed in Finnish, it is normally accepted as proof of sufficient language skills for citizenship purposes. There is no separate nationwide rule requiring 15 ECTS of Finnish language studies on top of a fully Finnish-taught degree.

The idea of “15 credits of Finnish” sometimes appears in specific institutional contexts (for example, internal graduation requirements or certain professional qualifications), but it is not a general immigration requirement for PR.

3. What About Vocational Education? Does It Count as Proof of Language Skills?

Yes, a vocational qualification completed in Finnish or Swedish can count as proof of language proficiency, particularly in the context of citizenship applications.

If you have completed:

• A vocational upper secondary qualification
• A further vocational qualification
• A specialist vocational qualification

and the qualification was completed in Finnish or Swedish, this can be accepted as proof of sufficient language skills instead of taking the YKI test.

There has not been a general removal of vocational qualifications as valid proof of language skills. However, the qualification must genuinely have been completed in Finnish or Swedish, not merely in Finland.

For permanent residence specifically, remember that language proof has not traditionally been required. The relevance of your vocational qualification depends on whether new language requirements for PR come into force.

4. Permanent Residence vs. Citizenship: Don’t Confuse the Two

A common source of misunderstanding is mixing up permanent residence rules with citizenship rules.

Permanent residence:
• Focuses on length of stay and permit type
• Traditionally has not required a language test
• May change in the near future

Citizenship:
• Requires a longer residence period
• Requires proof of language skills (usually B1 level)
• Accepts certain Finnish- or Swedish-language degrees as proof

If you are planning long-term residence, it is wise to prepare for citizenship-level language requirements even if PR currently does not require them.

5. What Should You Do If You’re Studying in Finnish Now?

If you are studying in Finnish at a university of applied sciences:

• Make sure your degree certificate clearly states that the language of instruction was Finnish
• Keep transcripts showing coursework completed in Finnish
• Consider whether your language level would meet at least B1 standard

If new PR language rules are introduced, they are likely to require at least basic functional ability (often A2 or B1 level). Completing an entire degree in Finnish would normally place you well above A2.

6. Final Practical Advice

Because immigration rules are currently in a period of reform, you should:

• Check Migri’s official website before applying
• Look at the exact legal text in force at the time of application
• Not rely solely on informal social media discussions
• Consider preparing for the YKI test if you plan to apply for citizenship later

In summary:

• A fully Finnish-taught UAS degree is generally sufficient proof of language ability when language proof is required.
• There is no general requirement for separate 15 ECTS of Finnish on top of a degree conducted in Finnish.
• Vocational qualifications completed in Finnish or Swedish remain valid proof of language skills in citizenship cases.
• Permanent residence has not historically required language proof, but upcoming reforms may introduce such a requirement.

If you are building your future in Finland, investing in solid Finnish language skills is beneficial regardless of the minimum legal requirement, both for immigration security and for long-term integration.

title: Permanent residence rules changed in January 2026: what it means if you applied in December 2025
description: A plain-English explainer of the timing, what “before vs after 8 Jan 2026” can affect, and what not to assume. If you submitted your permanent residence (PR) application in December 2025…
html:
A plain-English explainer of the timing, what “before vs after 8 Jan 2026” can affect, and what not to assume.

If you submitted your permanent residence (PR) application in December 2025 and completed your four years of continuous residence in early 2026, you are certainly not alone. Many applicants who applied toward the end of the year are now wondering the same thing: how long will the decision take, and has anyone with a similar timeline already received an answer?

This article explains how permanent residence processing works in Finland, what realistically affects your timeline, and what you can expect in the months following submission.

Understanding the Four-Year Requirement

For a permanent residence permit (P permit) based on work, you must have lived in Finland continuously for four years with a continuous (A) residence permit. The four-year period must be completed before a positive decision can be granted.

However, it is possible to submit your application slightly before reaching the four-year mark, as long as the requirement is fulfilled by the time the Finnish Immigration Service (Migri) makes its decision.

In your case:
– Application submitted: December 12, 2025
– Identity confirmed: December 15, 2025
– Four years completed: March 1, 2026

This timeline is generally acceptable. Migri will assess whether the four-year continuous residence requirement is fulfilled at the time of decision-making, not strictly at the time of submission.

Current Processing Times for Permanent Residence

Processing times for permanent residence permits in Finland vary depending on:

– Application volume
– Complexity of the case
– Whether additional documents are required
– Security or background checks
– Changes in immigration policy or staffing

In recent years, permanent residence applications have typically taken anywhere between 6 and 12 months to process. Some straightforward cases are decided faster, while others can take longer, particularly if:

– There have been gaps in residence permits
– Employment history needs clarification
– There were periods of unemployment or reliance on benefits
– Travel history requires review
– Additional documentation is requested

Applications submitted at the end of the year sometimes face slightly longer queues due to higher submission volumes before legislative or policy changes.

Have December 2025 Applicants Received Decisions Yet?

For applicants who submitted in December 2025, it would not be unusual if, by mid-2026, decisions are still pending. If processing is moving at an average pace of 8–10 months, decisions might reasonably be expected between late summer and autumn 2026.

That said, some applicants with very straightforward employment histories and no complications may receive decisions earlier. Others may wait longer if their case requires additional review.

It is important to understand that applications are not always processed strictly in chronological order. Migri may prioritize certain categories or cases based on internal workflow management.

What Factors Can Speed Up or Delay a Decision?

Several elements influence how quickly you receive a decision:

1. Continuous Employment

If you have been continuously employed and meet income requirements without interruption, your application is typically more straightforward.

2. No Gaps in Residence Permits

Any gaps between residence permits can complicate eligibility for permanent residence. Continuous (A) permits must have been valid throughout the four-year period.

3. No Criminal Record or Ongoing Investigations

Security checks are a routine part of the process. Clean records generally mean smoother processing.

4. Complete Documentation

If Migri does not need to request additional documents, your case moves faster. Requests for clarification can add weeks or months.

5. Travel Outside Finland

Short trips abroad are normal. However, extended stays outside Finland may trigger closer review to ensure continuous residence requirements are met.

What Happens After Identity Confirmation?

Once your identity has been confirmed at a service point, your application moves into substantive processing. There is usually no further action required from you unless:

– Migri requests additional documents
– Your employment situation changes
– Your passport expires
– Your contact details change

You can monitor your application status through the Enter Finland portal. However, status updates are often minimal until a decision is made.

Is It Normal Not to Hear Anything for Months?

Yes. It is entirely normal for there to be several months of silence after submission. Permanent residence applications do not usually involve interviews, and communication only occurs if additional information is needed.

No news generally means your application is waiting in queue or under review.

When Should You Be Concerned?

You should only consider following up if:

– Your application has significantly exceeded the published average processing time
– You receive a request for additional documents and have already submitted them long ago
– There is an urgent change in your legal status

Otherwise, waiting 8–12 months is within the normal range.

What You Can Do While Waiting

While your PR application is being processed:

– Ensure your current residence permit remains valid
– Keep your employment stable if possible
– Notify Migri of any major life changes
– Avoid long absences from Finland

If your current permit expires before a decision is made, you are generally allowed to continue living and working in Finland under the “extended permit” rule, provided you applied before expiry.

Realistic Expectations for December 2025 Applicants

Based on typical processing patterns:

– Early decisions: around 6–7 months (best-case, straightforward cases)
– Average decisions: around 8–10 months
– Longer cases: 12 months or more

For someone who applied in mid-December 2025 and completed the four-year requirement in March 2026, receiving a decision between August and October 2026 would fall well within normal expectations.

Final Thoughts

Waiting for permanent residence can feel stressful, especially after reaching the four-year milestone. However, if your residence has been continuous, your employment stable, and your documentation complete, there is generally little reason for concern.

Processing times vary, and comparing timelines with others can be helpful, but it is important to remember that every case is assessed individually.

For December 2025 applicants, patience is still part of the process. If your application is complete and your eligibility requirements are clearly met, the decision will come, most likely within the standard processing window.

If you would like help reviewing your specific timeline or identifying potential risk factors in your case, it can be useful to assess your residence history, permit types, and employment continuity in detail.

title: Renting Out Your Finnish Rivitalo: Can You Deduct the Mortgage Interest (or Only the Vastike)?
description: The quick answer Yes, in most normal situations you can deduct the interest on the loan used to buy the home once that home is being rented out (or you’re actively trying to rent it…
html:
The quick answer

Yes, in most normal situations you can deduct the interest on the loan used to buy the home once that home is being rented out (or you’re actively trying to rent it out). You usually do not need to renegotiate your loan into an “investment loan” with the bank for tax purposes. What matters is that the loan is connected to an asset that’s now producing taxable rental income, and that you claim the deductions for the correct period.

How rental income is taxed in Finland

Rental income is capital income. In 2026, the capital income tax rate is 30% up to €30,000, and 34% above that.

You’re taxed on the net amount: rent received minus deductible rental expenses.

What Vero means by “loan for the production of income”

This wording makes people think they needed a special loan type from day one. You didn’t.

Vero’s point is simpler: interest on loans for the production of income is deducted against capital income, including rental income, and bank charges related to that loan can also be deductible.

If you lived in the home yourself for years, the loan started life as a normal home loan. That part is fine. What changes is the use of the property.

When the interest becomes deductible (and what to do with “part of the year”)

Vero is very clear on timing:

  • Deductibility begins when you start your rental operation. That can be the lease start date, but it can also be earlier if you can show you started actively looking for tenants (first listing, agent contract, etc.).

  • You can only deduct expenses for the period the rental operation is ongoing. If you use the apartment for yourself, expenses aren’t deductible for that period.

So if you move out mid-year, it’s normal to split things by months.

Do you need to change the loan with the bank?

Usually, no.

This is mostly a tax reporting issue, not a bank-product issue. Vero says banks report interest info, and you should check/correct the entries in your tax return/MyTax as needed.

If your bank offers different margins for “investment loans”, that’s a financial choice. It isn’t the thing that decides tax deductibility.

What you can deduct from rental income (housing-company apartment)

For an apartment owned via housing-company shares, Vero lists deductions such as:

  • Maintenance charges (hoitovastike)

  • Water charges

  • Tenant search costs (ads, agent fees)

  • Property insurance

  • Certain travel expenses related to managing the rental (showings, signing lease, maintenance checks, shareholder meeting)

The big idea: if it’s a direct expense of renting, it’s usually deductible, but only for the rental period.

Hoitovastike vs rahoitusvastike (this one matters)

You already clocked hoitovastike. Easy.

Rahoitusvastike/pääomavastike (housing-company loan coverage) is the one that depends on accounting:

  • You can deduct it if the housing company treats it as annual revenue.

  • If it’s booked as a balance-sheet reserve, you can’t deduct it now, but you can add it to the acquisition cost and use it later when calculating capital gain on sale.

  • Some housing companies split it (part revenue, part balance sheet), so you only deduct the revenue part.

This is why people message their isännöitsijä and suddenly everything becomes clearer.

The “below-market rent” trap (where interest deductions can disappear)

If you rent the place out below market value, Vero limits deductions because it’s not considered renting “with an intent to gain income” in the normal sense.

In that case, Vero notes you cannot deduct the full expenses, and interest/bank fee deductions can be restricted.

If you want clean, predictable deductions: keep the rent broadly in line with market levels.

If your expenses are higher than the rent

Also common, especially with a mortgage.

Vero explains that if your rental expenses exceed rental income, the loss can be deducted against other capital income, and if you don’t have capital income, you may get a deficit credit (Vero uses a 30% credit example and also notes the annual maximum).

Reporting it properly (so you don’t end up fixing it later)

Vero is blunt here: all rental income and the expenses of renting must be reported, even if the income is low and even if deductions wipe it out.

If your rental starts during the year, it’s often worth adjusting prepayments/withholding so you don’t get a surprise bill later, but the key is simply: report the income and the expenses, and keep the dates/documentation tidy.

The bottom line for your situation

If:

  • you bought the rivitalo with a loan,

  • lived there for four years,

  • and now you’re renting it out at market rent,

then from the point the rental operation starts (or you can show you began actively looking for a tenant), the loan interest is generally deductible as an expense connected to producing rental income. You usually don’t need to change the bank loan product to make that “count”.

title: Teeth Cleaning in Finland’s Public Dental Care: What It Costs (and Why Everyone Pays Something Different)
description: The public fee is usually a basic visit charge plus procedure fees, so “just a clean” can mean very different totals. Here’s what’s normally included, what’s extra, and what to ask so…
html:
The public fee is usually a basic visit charge plus procedure fees, so “just a clean” can mean very different totals. Here’s what’s normally included, what’s extra, and what to ask so you know the cost before you sit down.

If you are living in Finland and wondering whether to book a dental cleaning through the public health care system, you are not alone. Many residents, both Finnish citizens and newcomers, ask how much it costs, how the system works, and whether it is worth using public dental services instead of private clinics.

Here is a clear, up‑to‑date overview of how teeth cleaning works in Finland’s public health care system, what you can expect to pay, and what factors influence the final price.

Is Teeth Cleaning Covered by Public Health Care in Finland?

Yes. Dental care is part of Finland’s public health care system and is available to all residents who are registered with a municipality (or wellbeing services county). This includes examinations, preventive care, and treatment such as fillings and periodontal care.

However, adult dental care is not free. You pay regulated client fees set by national legislation, and in many cases you also pay laboratory or procedure-specific fees.

For children under 18, dental care in the public system is generally free of charge.

How Much Does Teeth Cleaning Cost in Public Dental Care?

The price of teeth cleaning in Finland’s public health care system typically ranges between 30 and 90 euros per visit, depending on:

• The extent of cleaning needed
• Whether it is done by a dentist or a dental hygienist
• The time required
• The number of surfaces treated

In most routine cases, a standard tartar removal (scaling) appointment with a dental hygienist costs roughly 40–70 euros. If the cleaning is more extensive and requires longer treatment time, the cost can rise toward the higher end of that range.

If a dentist performs the cleaning instead of a hygienist, the fee may be somewhat higher.

Why the Price Varies

Public dental fees in Finland are based on a price list regulated by law. The final cost is calculated using specific procedure codes. For example:

• A basic oral examination is charged separately
• X-rays are charged separately
• Scaling is charged per 15-minute block
• Local anesthesia, if needed, may have its own small fee

This means that if you go in for a check-up and cleaning in the same visit, you will likely pay for both the examination and the cleaning.

As a rough total estimate:
• Examination: around 15–30 euros
• Dental hygienist cleaning: around 40–70 euros
• X-rays (if needed): around 10–20 euros

So a full visit with examination, cleaning, and X-rays might total approximately 70–120 euros.

Is There an Annual Maximum Fee?

Public dental care fees for adults are not usually included in the general health care annual payment cap (the “asiakasmaksukatto”) in the same way as doctor visits and hospital care. This means dental costs are typically paid separately and are not capped under the standard annual ceiling for health care fees.

However, fees are still significantly lower than private dental care.

How Does Public Compare to Private Dental Care?

In private clinics in Finland, a similar cleaning appointment often costs between 80 and 150 euros, and sometimes more depending on the city and clinic. Kela (the Social Insurance Institution of Finland) reimburses a small portion of private dental care costs, but you still pay much more out of pocket compared to public care.

So if cost is your primary concern, public dental care is usually considerably cheaper.

How Do You Book a Public Dental Appointment?

To use public dental services, you must contact your local health centre (terveysasema) or dental clinic in your wellbeing services county. Most areas require you to call for an initial assessment. In some regions, online booking is available.

Be aware that waiting times for non-urgent appointments can be long, sometimes several weeks or even months, especially in larger cities. Urgent cases are prioritized.

Is It Worth It?

For routine tartar removal and preventive care, public dental services in Finland are generally:

• Affordable
• Professionally delivered
• Regulated in price
• High in quality

The main downside is waiting time, not quality or cost.

If you are flexible about appointment timing and want to keep costs moderate, public dental care is a practical and financially sensible option.

Final Thoughts

If you are considering teeth cleaning through Finland’s public health care system, you can realistically expect to pay somewhere between 40 and 90 euros for a standard cleaning appointment, depending on how much work is needed and whether other procedures are done at the same time.

Compared to private clinics, this is significantly cheaper. For children, it is free. For adults, it remains reasonably priced by international standards.

If you are newly arrived in Finland and registered with a municipality, you are entitled to use these services. It is simply a matter of contacting your local public dental clinic and booking an appointment.

In short: yes, many residents use public dental care for teeth cleaning, and the cost is generally moderate and predictable.

title: VAT or No VAT as a Toiminimi? What to Do When a B2B Client “Insists”
description: If your turnover is under the threshold, you’re not forced to register, but clients often ask anyway. Here’s how VAT affects your pricing, invoicing, and what your customer can (and…
html:
If your turnover is under the threshold, you’re not forced to register, but clients often ask anyway. Here’s how VAT affects your pricing, invoicing, and what your customer can (and can’t) reclaim.

If you’ve recently set up a toiminimi (sole trader) in Finland, congratulations. One of the first practical questions you’ll face is whether to register for VAT (arvonlisävero, ALV). This becomes especially confusing when your turnover is low, but your business customers are asking you to register anyway.

Let’s break this down clearly and logically so you can make the right decision for your situation.

1. Do You Have to Register for VAT in Finland?

In Finland, VAT registration is mandatory if your annual turnover exceeds 15,000€ during a 12‑month accounting period. (This threshold applies under current rules; always check for updates, as VAT rules do change.)

If your turnover stays below 15,000€, you are not required to register for VAT. You can operate without adding VAT to your invoices.

However, even if you are below the threshold, you are allowed to register voluntarily.

2. What Happens If You Do NOT Register for VAT?

If you are not VAT registered:

• You do not add VAT to your invoices
• You cannot deduct VAT on your business purchases
• You are treated as selling VAT‑free services

If you invoice 1,500€, your client pays exactly 1,500€. No VAT is added.

For some small businesses, this keeps pricing simpler and potentially more competitive, especially if selling to private individuals (B2C customers), because they cannot deduct VAT.

But there is a downside: if you have significant business expenses that include VAT (equipment, software, rent, etc.), you cannot reclaim that VAT.

3. What Happens If You DO Register for VAT?

If you register for VAT, you must:

• Add VAT to your invoices (currently 25.5% for standard-rated services in Finland)
• Submit VAT returns regularly (monthly, quarterly, or annually depending on your setup)
• Pay collected VAT to the Tax Administration
• You can deduct VAT on your business purchases

Using your example:

Service price: 1,500€
VAT (25.5%): 382.50€
Total invoice: 1,882.50€

The 382.50€ is not your income. You are collecting it on behalf of the Finnish Tax Administration.

4. Can Your B2B Customer “Claim Back” the VAT?

Yes, but not in the way many people imagine.

If your customer is a VAT‑registered business in Finland:

• They deduct the VAT in their own VAT return
• They do not usually wait until the end of the fiscal year
• The deduction typically happens in their next VAT reporting period

So in practice, if you invoice 1,882.50€, the business customer treats 1,500€ as the cost and deducts the 382.50€ VAT from the VAT they owe.

For a VAT‑registered business, VAT is usually neutral. It does not increase their real cost.

This is often why B2B partners prefer you to be VAT registered. It keeps everything within the normal VAT system and avoids special handling.

5. Why Is Your B2B Partner Asking You to Register?

There are several possible reasons:

1. Administrative simplicity
Businesses are used to dealing with VAT-registered suppliers. Non‑VAT suppliers require separate accounting treatment.

2. Professional perception
Some companies associate VAT registration with a more established business.

3. Internal policy
Some larger firms prefer or require suppliers to be VAT registered.

4. Input VAT recovery expectations
They are used to deducting VAT and may prefer invoices structured in the standard VAT format.

From their perspective, if they can deduct the VAT, it does not increase their cost.

6. When Voluntary VAT Registration Makes Sense

Registering voluntarily may be a good idea if:

• Most of your customers are VAT‑registered businesses
• You have significant business expenses with VAT
• You expect your turnover to exceed 15,000€ soon
• Your clients are actively requesting VAT registration

In purely B2B situations, VAT often does not affect competitiveness because the customer deducts it.

7. When It Might Be Better Not to Register

Remaining outside VAT can make sense if:

• Your customers are private individuals (B2C)
• Your expenses are minimal
• You want to reduce administrative work
• You are testing a very small-scale side business

For private consumers, VAT increases the final price. If you add 25.5%, they cannot deduct it, so your service genuinely becomes more expensive for them.

8. Important: VAT Is Not Extra Income

One common misunderstanding is thinking that adding VAT increases your revenue.

It does not.

If you invoice 1,882.50€ including VAT, only 1,500€ is your business income. The rest belongs to the Tax Administration.

You must manage this cash carefully and set it aside, because you will need to pay it during your VAT reporting period.

9. A Quick Note About EU Cross-Border B2B Sales

If you are selling services to a VAT‑registered business in another EU country, the reverse charge mechanism may apply. In that case:

• You do not charge Finnish VAT
• The buyer accounts for VAT in their own country

This is a separate situation and depends on the type of service and the customer’s VAT number.

10. So What Should You Do?

Ask yourself three key questions:

1. Are my customers mostly businesses or consumers?
2. Do I have significant VAT on my expenses?
3. Am I likely to exceed 15,000€ turnover soon?

If you are primarily B2B and your partner prefers VAT registration, it often makes practical sense to register voluntarily. It usually does not financially disadvantage them, and it may simplify your working relationship.

If you are small-scale, mostly B2C, and have minimal expenses, staying outside VAT may keep things simpler and cheaper for your customers.

Final Thought

VAT registration is less about making more money and more about positioning your business correctly within the Finnish tax system.

For B2B services, VAT is usually neutral. For B2C services, it affects pricing significantly.

If in doubt, a short consultation with an accountant familiar with Finnish sole traders can save you time, money, and administrative stress later.

Understanding VAT early on is one of the best investments you can make in your Finnish business journey.

title: Waiting on a Spouse Extended Permit in Finland? Here’s What “Normal” Looks Like
description: Extended Residence Permit for the Spouse of a Non-EU National in Finland: Processing Times, Experiences and Expedited Requests If you are waiting for a decision on an extended residence…
html:
Extended Residence Permit for the Spouse of a Non-EU National in Finland: Processing Times, Experiences and Expedited Requests

If you are waiting for a decision on an extended residence permit as the spouse of a non-EU national in Finland, you are not alone. Many families find this period stressful, especially when there is an urgent need to travel abroad. In this article, I will explain what is currently known about processing times, what recent applicants have experienced, and how expedited processing works in practice.

Understanding the Extended Permit for Family Members

If you are in Finland as the spouse of a non-EU national, your residence permit is usually granted on the basis of family ties. When your first permit is about to expire, you must apply for an extended permit (jatkolupa).

The application is typically submitted through the Enter Finland online service. After submission, you must prove your identity, usually at a Finnish Immigration Service (Migri) service point if required. The decision is made by Migri.

Unlike first permits applied for abroad, extended permits are often processed inside Finland, and in many cases they are faster. However, “faster” does not mean immediate.

Recent Processing Times: What Applicants Are Experiencing

According to recent data published by the Finnish Immigration Service, the average processing time for extended residence permits based on family ties has typically ranged from 1 to 4 months. However, this is an average. Actual processing times vary depending on:

• Whether the application is complete
• Whether additional documents are requested
• The workload of the specific Migri unit
• Changes in family or financial circumstances
• Security or background checks

In practical terms, many recent applicants report decisions within approximately 6 to 12 weeks from the date of submitting a complete application online. Some have received decisions in as little as one month, especially if their situation has not changed and all documentation was clearly submitted.

Others have reported waiting closer to three or even four months, particularly if additional clarification was requested.

A typical timeline looks like this:

Application submitted online: mid-October
Identity verification (if required): within 1–2 weeks
Decision received: late December or January

Of course, there are also cases that take longer, especially if there are missing documents or complex circumstances.

Can You Travel While Waiting?

This is one of the most common concerns.

If you applied for your extended permit before your current permit expired, you are legally allowed to stay in Finland while waiting for the decision. However, travelling outside Finland (and especially outside the Schengen area) can be risky.

If your residence permit card expires while you are abroad, returning to Finland can be complicated. Airlines and border authorities may not accept proof of a pending application as sufficient documentation for entry. You may need a valid residence permit card to re-enter.

For urgent travel back home, it is essential to consider:

• Is your current residence permit still valid?
• Will it expire before you return?
• Do you require a visa to enter Finland?

If your card expires while you are outside Finland, you may need to apply for a D visa or a return visa from a Finnish mission abroad, which can delay your return significantly.

Requesting Expedited Processing: Is It Possible?

Migri does allow requests for expedited processing (urgent processing), but these are only accepted under very specific and serious circumstances.

You cannot simply request expedited handling because you want to travel. The reasons must usually involve:

• Serious illness or death of a close family member
• A critical family emergency
• Significant employer-related urgency (in certain work-related permits)
• Humanitarian grounds

Wanting to visit family, attend a wedding, or deal with general travel plans is usually not considered sufficient grounds.

How to Request Expedited Processing

To request expedited handling, you must:

1. Submit your application normally.
2. Send a written request explaining the urgent reason.
3. Provide strong supporting documentation (for example, a hospital certificate, medical report, or official document confirming the emergency).

Migri evaluates expedited requests individually. In practice, only a small proportion are accepted.

Recent applicants who have requested expedited processing report mixed outcomes:

• Requests based on serious medical emergencies have sometimes been accepted.
• Requests based solely on travel plans or general urgency are usually declined.
• Some applicants receive no formal “acceptance” of expedition, but their case may be handled slightly faster if documentation is clear and complete.

If your request is denied, your application continues under normal processing time.

What Actually Helps Speed Up the Process?

While you cannot control Migri’s workload, you can reduce the risk of delays:

• Submit all required documents at once.
• Ensure income requirements are clearly met (if applicable).
• Attach up-to-date employment contracts or payslips.
• Make sure your passport is valid.
• Respond immediately to any additional information requests.

Incomplete applications are one of the most common causes of delay.

Realistic Expectations for 2026

Based on current trends, most extended family permits for spouses of non-EU nationals are processed within approximately 2–3 months if there are no complications.

Some are faster. Some take longer.

It is uncommon for straightforward extended permits to take more than 5–6 months unless:

• There are changes in the relationship status
• Financial requirements are not clearly met
• There are identity or background issues
• Documents are missing

If you have already been waiting longer than the published average processing time on Migri’s website, you may submit a request for information, but this does not automatically speed up the case.

If You Urgently Need to Travel Home

If you urgently need to travel due to a genuine emergency:

1. Check your current residence permit expiry date immediately.
2. If still valid for the full duration of your trip, travel may be possible.
3. If it will expire while you are abroad, consider carefully whether travel is worth the re-entry risk.
4. If the reason is serious, submit an expedited processing request with full documentation.
5. Contact Migri’s customer service for guidance specific to your situation.

Do not rely solely on informal online advice when making travel decisions. Entry rules can change and individual circumstances matter greatly.

Final Thoughts

Waiting for an extended residence permit decision can feel overwhelming, especially when family emergencies arise. The good news is that most extended permits for spouses of non-EU nationals in Finland are processed within a few months, and many applicants receive decisions within 1–3 months.

Expedited processing is possible but reserved for truly serious situations and requires strong documentation. Travel while waiting carries risks, especially if your residence permit card expires.

If you are in an urgent situation, act quickly, gather official documents, and communicate clearly with Migri. And if your application is complete and your circumstances are stable, there is a strong likelihood that your decision will arrive within the normal processing window.

Patience is difficult during uncertainty, but in most straightforward cases, extended permits are granted without major issues.
